seoTitle: Sepsis Management Algorithm: Fluids, Pressors, Antibiotics
metaDescription: Septic shock in the ED, fork by fork: antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, norepinephrine to a MAP of 65, meningitis and neutropenic fever.
h1: Sepsis and septic shock management: the ED algorithm, fork by fork
dek: For the student on an EM or IM rotation with a septic patient and a resident about to ask what is next: the screen, the first hour, pressors, source control, meningitis and neutropenic fever, what to say on rounds, and what you will be pimped on.

shortAnswer.lead: Screen with SIRS, NEWS or MEWS and a lactate.
shortAnswer.text: qSOFA is not recommended as a single screening tool, and a lactate alone neither rules sepsis in nor out. Procalcitonin does not decide when antibiotics start.
Cultures first only if that delays the antibiotics less than 45 minutes. Possible sepsis without shock gets a rapid workup and antibiotics within 3 hours if the concern persists.

shortAnswer.lead: At least 30 mL/kg of crystalloid for hypoperfusion.
shortAnswer.text: Balanced crystalloid over saline, within the first 3 hours, by actual weight (adjusted or ideal if BMI over 30); albumin only after large crystalloid volumes, starches never. NICE NG253 gives 250 mL boluses instead, up to 1,000 mL, reassessing after each.
60 to 65 at 65 or older. Start it peripherally rather than wait for a central line; dopamine is not first line.

MAP below target on norepinephrine 0.25 mcg/kg/min or more: add vasopressin at a fixed 0.03 units/min, and IV hydrocortisone 200 mg a day (SSC 2021 at least 4 hours in; SSC 2026 broadened it); epinephrine next if the MAP is still inadequate.

shortAnswer.lead: Find the source and control it.
shortAnswer.text: Image the kidneys now in urinary sepsis, debride necrotizing infection as soon as possible, at the latest within 6 hours of admission, and remove a suspected line once other access is in.

The LP comes first only with no CT criterion, no contraindication and no delay. Otherwise blood cultures, dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and antibiotics go in before the CT. Listeria risk adds ampicillin or amoxicillin.

shortAnswer.lead: Fever within 6 weeks of chemotherapy is treated as neutropenic infection.
shortAnswer.text: Assess within 15 minutes, first antibiotic within 1 hour: an antipseudomonal beta-lactam alone, with vancomycin only for line, skin, pneumonia or instability. MASCC 21 or more, with no clinical exclusion and home supports in place, can go home after a first dose and 4 hours of observation.

sections.heading: How do you screen for sepsis, and what goes in during the first hour?
sections.intro: Score the vitals and draw a lactate; then cultures, antibiotics and fluid run together. Meningitis features in shock add dexamethasone with the first antibiotic and defer the LP.

sections.heading: Septic shock, sepsis or neither: how do the findings sort the patient?
sections.intro: Each fork reads one result: the first look, the MAP after fluid and on norepinephrine, the source, the CT and CSF, Listeria risk and the ANC.

sections.heading: Which vasopressor and which antibiotics in septic shock?
sections.intro: Norepinephrine first and vasopressin before escalating it; the antibiotic regimen then follows the source: pneumonia, skin, line, meningitis or neutropenia.

sections.heading: When do you image the kidneys in urosepsis?
sections.intro: Now, in sepsis, for an obstruction or abscess that needs drainage. Antibiotics never wait for the scan.

sections.heading: When does the LP come before antibiotics in suspected meningitis?
sections.intro: Only when it is safe and quick. The same stage covers possible sepsis with infection uncertain, and sepsis with no source found.

sections.heading: What do you do in the first hour of neutropenic fever?
sections.intro: Assess within 15 minutes, draw at least two sets of blood cultures and baseline labs, and give the first antibiotic within 1 hour.

sections.heading: Who can go home with neutropenic fever, pyelonephritis or cellulitis?
sections.intro: Low-risk febrile neutropenia after a first dose and 4 hours of observation; pyelonephritis without sepsis that is taking oral fluids; early, mild cellulitis on an oral beta-lactam.

sections.heading: Where does each septic patient end up?
sections.intro: Every branch ends on a named diagnosis and its plan, from the drained obstructed kidney to the non-infectious mimic whose antibiotics stop.

checklist.heading: The first hour: what has to be done

items.text: Vitals scored with SIRS, NEWS or MEWS, and a blood lactate.
Blood cultures, if they delay the antibiotics less than 45 minutes.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour; MRSA cover only at high MRSA risk.
At least 30 mL/kg of IV balanced crystalloid within 3 hours for hypoperfusion (NICE NG253: 250 mL boluses, up to 1,000 mL); repeat the lactate.
MAP under 65 after the fluid (under 60 at 65 or older): norepinephrine, peripherally until a central line.
A source that needs emergent control identified or excluded.
Meningitis features: dexamethasone 10 to 20 minutes before or with the first antibiotic.
Chemotherapy in the last 6 weeks: assessed within 15 minutes, two sets of blood cultures.

rounds.present: 71-year-old woman with septic shock from an infected, obstructed right kidney after 2 days of fever and right flank pain, now confused. Shock: lactate 5.4; 2 L of balanced crystalloid, at least 30 mL/kg at 64 kg, left a MAP of 56, so norepinephrine was started peripherally. Still on 0.3 mcg/kg/min with a MAP of 54 at 4 hours, so vasopressin 0.03 units/min is added and IV hydrocortisone 200 mg a day. Source: right costovertebral angle tenderness, nitrite-positive urine with many white cells, and right hydronephrosis behind a 9 mm proximal ureteric stone. Urine culture before antibiotics; IV antibiotics running. Plan: urgent drainage, where ACR rates percutaneous nephrostomy usually appropriate for a septic, hypotensive patient.

pimp.a: It is not recommended as a single screening tool compared with SIRS, NEWS or MEWS.
Against dopamine, norepinephrine had lower mortality and fewer arrhythmias.

pimp.q: Why not push the MAP to 85?
pimp.a: Higher targets did not improve survival. The initial target is 65, or 60 to 65 at 65 or older.

pimp.q: Why does a pregnant patient with meningitis get ampicillin?
pimp.a: Listeria is intrinsically resistant to third-generation cephalosporins. Pregnancy, immunocompromise and age over 50 (IDSA) or over 60 (WHO 2025) add ampicillin or amoxicillin.

pimp.q: Why not a CT before every LP?
pimp.a: Routine imaging before LP is not recommended, and LP without a prior CT was associated with lower mortality than LP after CT. The CT is for the CT criteria.

pimp.q: Why not add an aminoglycoside in high-risk neutropenic fever?
pimp.a: It brought more toxicity and no better survival. Antipseudomonal beta-lactam monotherapy is recommended.

traps.text: qSOFA alone, or a normal lactate, as the reason to stop worrying. qSOFA is not a single screening tool, and a lactate alone neither rules sepsis in nor out.
Holding antibiotics until the source is confirmed or imaged. In probable sepsis or shock they go in within 1 hour, and imaging never comes first.
Albumin or starch as the opening fluid. Crystalloid is first line, albumin only after large crystalloid volumes, starches never.
CT, then LP, then antibiotics. When the LP has to wait, blood cultures, dexamethasone and antibiotics go in first.
A plain film, a CT or a low LRINEC before calling surgery for necrotizing signs. Imaging must not delay debridement, and a low LRINEC does not rule it out.
Vancomycin as standard in febrile neutropenia. It is kept for suspected catheter infection, skin or soft tissue infection, pneumonia or hemodynamic instability.
Treating through an infected central line. Get other vascular access, then remove it promptly.
Ceftriaxone alone for meningitis at 68 or in pregnancy. Listeria needs ampicillin or amoxicillin added.

faq.q: What is in the first hour of sepsis treatment?
faq.a: For probable sepsis or shock: blood cultures if they delay antibiotics less than 45 minutes, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, and at least 30 mL/kg of IV balanced crystalloid within 3 hours for hypoperfusion, with a repeat lactate. Norepinephrine can start during the fluid if the shock is unstable. NICE NG253 gives 250 mL boluses, up to 1,000 mL in all, instead of the 30 mL/kg.

faq.q: What MAP target is used in septic shock?
faq.a: An initial MAP of 65 mm Hg, or 60 to 65 for adults 65 or older; higher targets did not improve survival. Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor, started peripherally for a short period in a vein at or above the antecubital fossa rather than waiting for a central line.

faq.q: When do you add vasopressin and hydrocortisone in septic shock?
faq.a: When the MAP stays below target on norepinephrine 0.25 mcg/kg/min or more: add vasopressin at a fixed 0.03 units/min rather than escalating the norepinephrine, and IV hydrocortisone 200 mg a day, 50 mg every 6 hours. SSC 2021 started the steroid at least 4 hours in; SSC 2026 broadened it to septic shock. Epinephrine comes next if the MAP is still inadequate.

faq.q: Do you need a CT before the LP in suspected meningitis?
faq.a: Not routinely. Image first only for a CT criterion: altered consciousness, focal signs, papilledema, a new seizure, immunocompromise or CNS disease. IDSA images for any abnormal level of consciousness; WHO (GCS under 10) and NICE (9 or less) are narrower. When the LP has to wait, blood cultures, dexamethasone and antibiotics go in first.

faq.q: What is the empiric antibiotic regimen for bacterial meningitis?
faq.a: IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus vancomycin, with dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours, the first dose 10 to 20 minutes before or with the first antibiotic. Add ampicillin or amoxicillin for Listeria risk: over 50 (IDSA) or over 60 (WHO 2025), pregnancy or immunocompromise. WHO adds vancomycin only where resistant pneumococci are common.

faq.q: What antibiotics are used for febrile neutropenia?
faq.a: High risk: admit for an IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam alone (cefepime, meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin or piperacillin-tazobactam) within 1 hour, with vancomycin only for line, skin, pneumonia or instability. Low risk, MASCC 21 or more with no exclusion and home supports: first dose in the ED, at least 4 hours of observation, then oral ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate.
